analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder and costlier for individuals to erase debts in bankruptcy, shifting power toward lenders.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and never received a hearing or vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the bankruptcy code along the lines the credit industry had sought for years. It would add a rigid 'means test' that presumes abuse whenever a debtor's income is above the state median, forcing some people out of Chapter 7 (which erases most debts) and into Chapter 5-year repayment plans [S3]. It would require everyone to get paid credit counseling before filing, cap the homestead exemption that protects a family's home, extend the time between discharges, and give secured lenders and financial-contract counterparties new protections [S3]. It also carries genuine consumer provisions: child support claims move to the front of the line, protections for retirement and education savings, tools against predatory lenders, and a permanent renewal of the family-farmer bankruptcy chapter [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card issuers, banks, and other consumer lenders gain the most: a means test that pushes more filers into partial repayment, mandatory credit counseling, tougher standards for repeat filings, longer intervals between discharges, and limits on the homestead exemption all mean more debts get paid instead of erased [S3]. Secured creditors such as auto and mortgage lenders get 'fair treatment' in Chapter 13, faster relief from the automatic stay, and rules on how collateral is valued [S3]. Counterparties to derivatives and other financial contracts gain new protections when an insured bank fails [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card issuers and secured lenders

how_it_helps.text: Adds a formula-based presumption of abuse: if a debtor's income above state median, minus IRS-standard expenses, exceeds set thresholds over 60 months, the case is presumed abusive and can be dismissed or converted to a repayment plan [S3].
Requires every individual filer to complete a briefing from an approved nonprofit credit counseling agency within 180 days before filing, and a financial management course before discharge [S3].

Includes a package of consumer-side provisions: domestic support (child support and alimony) claims get priority and become harder to discharge; retirement savings and education savings are shielded in bankruptcy; purchasers of predatory loans cannot strip the debtor's claims and defenses; and insolvent health care businesses must appoint a patient-advocate ombudsman [S2] [S3].
Permanently reenacts Chapter 12 for family farmers, raises its debt limit, eases the definition of a family farmer, and brings family fishermen under the same protection [S2] [S3].

Gives counterparties to qualified financial contracts new rights when an insured depository institution fails or enters receivership, and adds a cross-border insolvency chapter modeled on the international Model Law [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People filing for bankruptcy. Those above their state's median income would face a presumption of abuse that can only be rebutted with documented 'special circumstances' under oath, pushing many into Chapter 13 plans that can run five years instead of wiping debts in a few months [S3]. Every filer would pay for credit counseling and a financial management course before being allowed relief [S3]. Consumer bankruptcy attorneys would face fee liability and civil penalties if a court finds their filings abusive, raising the cost and risk of representation [S3]. State flexibility to shield a home through homestead exemptions would be capped [S3].

drawbacks.text: The means test replaces a judge's discretion with a formula: a debtor above median income is presumed abusive and must document and attest to special circumstances to rebut the presumption, which pushes many honest filers into multi-year repayment plans [S3].
Mandatory pre-filing credit counseling and pre-discharge financial management courses add fees and delay for everyone, including debtors in obvious hardship, subject to narrow waivers [S3].

The bill strengthens creditor positions: secured creditors get 'fair treatment' in Chapter 13, faster relief from the automatic stay when a debtor fails to surrender collateral, and stricter rules on valuing and keeping collateral — making it harder for families to keep homes and cars [S3].
Debt relief agencies and consumer bankruptcy attorneys face new restrictions, disclosure mandates, and fee liability, which raises the price of getting legal help to file [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's creditor-facing gains are concrete and large: a means test, counseling mandates, and secured-creditor protections measurably shift the system toward repayment and away from discharge. Its genuine consumer provisions — child support priority, retirement and education savings protection, predatory-loan defenses, permanent family-farmer relief — are real but modest, and several are partly offset by the new burdens (counseling fees, means-test documentation, longer plans, attorney liability) placed on the very people seeking relief. An honest supporter would say the bill targets a minority of high-income repeat filers; an honest opponent would answer that it taxes everyone who files to chase that minority.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-November 2002 and sent to the House Judiciary and Financial Services Committees, and both sat on it until the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 — no hearing, no markup, no vote, no cosponsors ever added.

narrative.text: Rep. George Gekas (R-PA) introduced the bill on November 14, 2002, in the closing weeks of the 107th Congress [S1] [S5].

It was referred to the Judiciary Committee and, for provisions in its jurisdiction, to the Financial Services Committee — the standard first step that gives committees control over whether a bill ever moves [S5].
The bill drew zero cosponsors and no further action of any kind appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, the existing bankruptcy rules stayed in place through the 107th Congress, so people who might have filed under the current, more flexible system came out ahead. The credit industry gained nothing from this bill — it had to continue pressing for a means-test law in the next Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday debtors, for one more Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill attracted no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan split — only a single Republican sponsor and two committees that never acted.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The means test, counseling mandate, longer discharge intervals, and anti-repeat-filer rules would push more debtors into paying unsecured debts instead of erasing them — the industry's gain comes directly out of what distressed households walk away with.

industries.industry: Secured creditors (auto, mortgage, and other collateralized lenders)
industries.note: New provisions give secured creditors 'fair treatment' in Chapter 13, faster relief from the automatic stay, and favorable collateral valuation rules, making it easier to collect on homes and cars secured by loans.

The bill makes a briefing from an approved nonprofit counseling agency a mandatory gateway before anyone can file, guaranteeing every bankruptcy filer becomes a paying customer of the counseling industry it sets standards for.

industries.industry: Consumer bankruptcy attorneys and debt relief agencies
industries.note: New restrictions, disclosure mandates, and attorney fee liability would raise the cost and legal risk of representing bankruptcy filers, whose interests these lawyers serve.
Title IX strengthens the rights of counterparties to qualified financial contracts when an insured bank fails, protecting their positions ahead of other claimants in receivership.
Permanent reenactment of Chapter 12 with a higher debt limit and relaxed eligibility keeps a purpose-built bankruptcy route open for small farming and fishing operations.
